subject: Business Models
title: Subway's Expansion Trap
description: A quick, practical guide to Subway's Expansion Trap.

hook.text: Subway hit 44,000 locations in 2015—more than McDonald's. Then it closed 7,000 stores in four years.

buildup.text: Subway's franchise fee was just $15,000 with no territory protection, attracting thousands of owners.

discovery.text: Without territory limits, new Subways opened next to existing ones. Owners cannibalized each other's sales.

twist.text: The franchisor profited from every new opening—fees and royalties. Individual franchisee losses didn't matter.

climax.text: Over-expansion destroyed unit economics. Average Subway revenue dropped 25% as saturation increased.

punchline.text: 44,000 stores, 7,000 closed. Growth without discipline destroys value.

quiz.question: What caused Subway's massive store closures?

details.summary: Subway became the world's largest restaurant chain by unit count through extremely low franchise fees and aggressive expansion. But oversaturation meant many locations were too close together, cannibalizing each other's sales..
details.whyItMatters: Subway's expansion trap is the definitive example of franchise quantity over quality. The franchisor earned more fees from more units while individual franchisees suffered declining revenue from oversaturation..
takeaways: Subway became the largest chain by unit count through very low franchise fees
Aggressive expansion led to locations cannibalizing each other's customer base
Franchisor revenue grew from more units while per-unit franchisee income declined

faq.question: How many Subway locations were there at peak expansion?
faq.answer: Subway peaked at over 44,000 locations worldwide, more than any other restaurant chain. In the US alone, there were more Subways than McDonald's. Since then, thousands of underperforming locations have closed as the company rationalized its footprint.

faq.question: Why did Subway prioritize unit count over unit profitability?
faq.answer: Subway earned franchise fees on each new opening and royalties on total system revenue. More units meant more fees regardless of whether individual stores were profitable. The franchisor's economics rewarded quantity while franchisees bore the costs of cannibalization.
